title: A Pop-Up Debate for Helping Students Value Writing
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave describes a classroom procedure built around Paul Graham's essay "Putting Ideas Into Words" and its implicit claim that writing is necessary for fully formed thought, turning that claim into a structured Pop-Up Debate. He walks through an eight-step sequence, hook, essay framing, annotated reading, pair-share, and the debate itself, designed to build comprehension of a challenging text while also building students' sense that writing is worth valuing, regardless of which side of the debate they land on.
points: Builds an entire lesson around a single implicit claim in a mentor text (writing is necessary for fully formed thought), using student disagreement itself as the engine for engagement.
Provides a concrete eight-step sequence, hook, framing, annotated reading, pair-share, and Pop-Up Debate rules, that other teachers can lift directly into their own classrooms.
Restates Pop-Up Debate's core participation rules (everyone speaks at least once, stand to speak, yield the floor politely) as a lightweight structure that doesn't require special training to run.

Argues the debate's real payoff isn't which side wins but that every student is forced to seriously think or argue about writing, positioning the exercise as a Value-building move rather than just a comprehension check.
quotes: But in one of the essays I read, Graham made a fascinating, implicit claim: the reason he's smart is because he writes.
Students, I know of a guy who claims that if you don't write about things then you'll never have a fully formed thought. In your whole life.
Every speaks at least 1x. To speak, stand up and start talking. If multiple people do this simultaneously, politely yield the floor.
When you give students an essay as well-written and well-argued as Graham's, you're certainly going to have students disagree with him.
And everyone, no matter which stance they took, will have given some serious thought to writing — a starting point for Value if every I've heard of one.
